steps.title: Database bottleneck
steps.caption: Every seat check is a database query, so adding app servers only pushes the database to 100%.
steps.body: Ticket sales open at 10:00 and 200,000 users arrive for 50,000 seats. The app servers keep no data, so every seat check and every reservation is a database query, and the two servers the autoscaler adds only send more of them. The database reaches 100% CPU with lock waits, and the p95 response time climbs to seconds.

steps.title: In-memory units
steps.caption: Units load the seats into memory and answer from it; the data grid copies A-12 to unit 2.
steps.body: Each **processing unit** is the application plus an in-memory copy of the data it needs, here the seat map, which a **data reader** loads from the database when the units start. The **messaging grid** routes each request to a unit, which answers from memory with no database call. When unit 1 sells A-12, the **data grid** replicates the change to unit 2 within milliseconds.

steps.title: Asynchronous writes
steps.caption: Each change also goes onto a data pump; a data writer updates the database in the background.
steps.body: Every change also goes onto a **data pump**, an asynchronous queue, and a **data writer** applies it to the database in the background. Nothing on the request path waits for the database: it becomes the durable record instead of the working store, and it is read only when units start with empty memory.

steps.title: Elastic, with trade-offs
steps.caption: The deployment manager runs 2 to 8 units. Units 1 and 2 both sold B-7: a data collision.
steps.body: As users arrive, the **deployment manager** starts units (from 2 up to 8), each copying the seats from a peer before it serves, and stops them after the rush. The costs: units 1 and 2 both sold B-7 before either update replicated (a **data collision**; give each section one owning unit, or detect and resolve conflicts), the replicated data must fit in every unit's memory, the database lags behind, and a crash before a change reaches a durable queue loses it. It suits spiky, high-concurrency workloads such as ticketing, auctions and flash sales, not large data sets that need complex queries.
